## **The Light on the Balcony (Additional Scene: The Tarmac)**

We were coming into Atlanta when Martin pulled me aside. He gripped my shoulder the way he always did—firm, fatherly, grounding.  

“Spot, I’ve heard about these threatening letters you’ve been receiving.”  

“Eh, don’t worry about it, Martin,” I said, waving it off.  

“I *am* worried about it,” he replied. “These are dangerous times we live in. I want you to ride with Abernathy to the rally.”  

“But Martin, I *always* ride with you. I’m not afraid of these yahoos. Hell, I grew up among them in Memphis.”  

“Son,” he said, giving my shoulder a gentle pinch of affection, “that doesn’t matter today. It’s important that *you* not receive any violence during this movement.”  

“Why?” I asked, confused but touched by his concern.  

He smiled that soft, knowing smile of his—the one that could calm a storm.  

“Because you have an important part to play. When history looks back at the pictures of our movement, they need to see a young white fella with kind eyes and a gentle smile standing next to me. I want little white children to see themselves in you when they think about the cause of race relations—and I want little black children to be inspired by you. When we Negroes march across this nation, I want them to see that a sweet, gentle white man, moved only by conviction and love for his fellow man, stood shoulder to shoulder with us.”  

I thought then of when he called Nichelle Nichols and pleaded with her to stay on *Star Trek*—how he told her she was living proof that Black people belonged in the future right alongside white people.  

“You got it, Martin,” I said quietly.  

He gave my shoulder one last squeeze, that familiar twinkle of faith in his eyes, and then turned toward the tarmac. I watched him stride toward the waiting motorcade, his coat flaring behind him like the hem of a prophet’s robe.

## **The Light on the Balcony (Car Ride on Poplar Avenue)**

“Well, Spot,” Martin said as we drove down Poplar Avenue in Memphis, “are you happy to be back in your hometown?”  

“Sure,” I said. “It lets me see my cat—and my folks.”  

“You have a cat?” Martin asked, surprised.

“Very adorable,” he said with a grin. “And that explains a lot.”  

“What does it explain?” I asked, sensing a jab coming.  

“Why I sneeze so much around you!”  

Kyles, Jackson, and Martin all cracked up, and I couldn’t help joining them.  

“Well, now,” I said, “it’s a good thing I was sick at the hotel the day you got stabbed at your book signing, Martin.”  

“Oh?”  

I cleared my throat and slipped into my best impression of his pulpit cadence.  

*“If I had merely sneezed, I would not have witnessed Spot tell that police chief to blow it out his ass. If I had sneezed, I would not have had that delightful cheeseburger for breakfast today. If I had merely sneezed, ladies and gentlemen—!”*  

I finished with a flourish, mimicking his rapturous, mystical timbre. Everyone guffawed and wheezed, including Martin himself. He slapped me across the shoulder with the back of his hand, laughing through tears.  

“Nix that, you dumb fool!” he said, barely able to breathe.  

Still chuckling, I leaned forward to Jackson at the wheel. “Turn onto Mount Moriah. There’s a donut shop there that has the best donuts in the city. It’s the next left at the Mendenhall–Mount Moriah split.”

Matteo sat in the office chair, drunk and disheveled. His bottle of Caribbean rum was nearly empty, his shirt was stained and untidy. He ran his hand through his unkempt hair. His stomach turned over and over. He sipped the last of the rum, hoping it would stop the prickling on the back of his neck. The door opened behind him, and he felt a rush of relief. At last, he could offload his troubles on an ally who could reverse his financial black hole.

"Señor Secretary, my accounts, they..." but when Matteo turned around, he did not see the Adjutant Financial Secretary of the Justicialist Party. The man at the door wore his clothes, but his face was one of the past. Matteo's eyes widened and blinked hard as if to ward off a nightmare he had tumbled into.

"It's time to answer for Juan Fernández, Matteo."

*It was Juan Fernández.* Matteo Herrera was not dreaming. Fernández walked to the back of the office and sat at the desk of the Adjutant Financial Secretary of the Justicialist Party, the local representative of Juan and Eva Perón out in the sticks of Los Toldos.

"You are alive," was all Matteo could choke out of his suddenly dry mouth.

"I never died," said Fernández, peering coldly from his piercing blue eyes over steepled fingers.

Matteo swallowed again and again and slowly recovered. "So...you are the orchestrator of my misery. My money...my reputation..."

"No," said Fernández, closing his eyes for a few seconds as he did.

"Do not lie to me, Juan Fernández," Matteo Herrera spat. "It was you as the accursed Financial Secretary who coaxed me to speculate my money! It was *you* who caused me to go on the run to this backwater town! I am on the *run,* and it's because of *you!"*

Fernández opened his eyes - those cold, blue, pitiless eyes. "I may have set up the dominos. It was *you* who knocked the first one over."

Matteo scoffed wryly. "You were never smart enough for such a set up. Who backed you? Who is pulling your strings, *pinche concho?!"*

"I am not the same hapless buffoon you helped frame for murder and sent to that island prison fifteen years ago. Why, I even know my letters. I am quite skilled at the financial calculus of the market. As to any benefactors, I merely had starting capital bequeathed to me by a friend in prison. The rest was successfully speculated under various names and various associations playing against each other."

Matteo, in spite of himself, hung his jaw open. "You are right. You are not that boorish hanger on from fifteen years ago. You are a monster."

"I am a divine arbiter of justice," said Fernández, waving away the title as if it was a fly. "The people who stole my life, my love, my family will merely find justice in an undoing of their own making, just as you have, Matteo. You thought you sent a buffoon to prison, so you could steal his job, his fiancé, and his life. He has come back to you in various forms to coax you into undoing the life you stole from him."

# Polished rewrite
Matteo sat slumped in the office chair, drunk and unkempt. His bottle of Caribbean rum was nearly empty; his shirt clung to him in dark, sticky patches. He ran a hand through his hair until it stuck in his palm. His stomach rolled. He tipped the bottle back and swallowed the last hot ribbon of rum, hoping it would quiet the prickling at the nape of his neck.

The door eased open. Relief uncoiled in him — at last, someone to share the weight of his disaster. “Señor Secretary, my accounts, they—” He turned.

The man in the doorway wore the Secretary’s suit, but the face that filled the frame was older, terrible and familiar. Matteo blinked as if the room had gone unreal.

“It’s time to answer for Juan Fernández, Matteo.”

Fernández crossed the office and sat where the Adjutant Financial Secretary always sat, as if reclaiming the chair itself were part of the sentence. Matte o’s mouth dried. “You’re—alive.”

“I never died.” Fernández’s voice was small and cold. He steepled his fingers and watched Matteo with pale, pitiless eyes.

Matteo found his voice in fits. “You caused this. You, as the Financial Secretary—you pushed me into those speculations. You ruined me. I’m on the run because of you.”

Fernández closed his eyes for a measured beat, then opened them again. “I may have set the dominos.” He smiled—no warmth in it. “But it was you who knocked the first one over.”

Matteo laughed, a sound that was half choke. “You? You weren’t clever enough. Who backed you? Who’s pulling your strings, pinche concho?” He spat the insult like a prayer.

“I’m not the fool you shipped to that island prison fifteen years ago.” Fernández’s hands were calm. “I learned to read ledgers in a place you’d call hell. I learned the mathematics of ruin. Starting capital came from a friend who owed a debt. The rest—was patient work across names and accounts. People like you don’t notice the slow tilt until the table falls.”

Matteo’s jaw slackened. “You are a monster.”

“I prefer arbiter,” Fernández corrected. “Those who stole my life will suffer by the rules they taught me. You thought you could bury a man and take his life. You dug a shallow grave. He crawled out.”

# Suggested continuation
Fernández tapped the desk, a staccato that sounded like dominoes falling. “There’s a list,” he said. “Names. Dates. Amounts. Every hand that helped itself to what belonged to me.” He reached into his jacket and produced a folded notebook. Matteo’s fingers went cold. He remembered the fiancé he’d taken, the promotion he’d pocketed, the party celebrations that smelled of other people’s futures.

“You could give it back,” Fernández continued, voice even. “You could confess to the papers, to the families, return what you can. Maybe that buys you something like mercy.” He leaned forward. “Or you could keep the stolen money and watch what returns to its owners. Justice is patient. So am I.”

Matteo’s laughter came again, thinner. “And if I refuse?”

Fernández’s smile widened like a blade. “Then the dominoes fall without you. I will not lift a finger. The world will do my work for me.” He tapped the ledger. “You will lose more than money, Matteo. You will lose the story you told yourself to sleep at night.”

The warning hung in the stagnant air. Matteo’s hand drifted—toward the top drawer, toward something he’d never meant to use. He froze, seeing himself from someone else’s angle: the man who stole another life and hid behind ledgers and lies. The bottle rolled from his fingers and shattered against the floor. “These,” he said, tapping the board, “are cribs. Predictable text. Phrases the Germans use constantly. Sign-offs, weather headers, boilerplate status lines.”

He turned back to them.

“Find these patterns in your old decrypts. Look for message lengths that match. Look for repeated phrase positions—line breaks, sign-offs, the places where naval captains get lazy and write the same thing every morning.”

Evelyn’s eyes lit up. “If we can guess even a few plaintext segments in the new messages—”

“—we can reverse-engineer the new settings,” Gareth finished, breath catching with excitement.

“Exactly,” Bernard said.

He lifted a stack of old decrypts and let them fan out between his fingers like a deck of cards.

“The Germans may have new keys. But they have old habits.”

A murmur of renewed purpose rippled through the room.

Bernard set the chalk down and straightened his jacket.

“We break this the old way—by wit, not luck. By patterns, not codebooks.”  
He met each pair of eyes.  
“And by refusing to be afraid of the dark.”

The breakers surged back to their desks—rifling through old decrypts, circling repeated phrases, measuring text lengths, scribbling potential alignments. A new kind of controlled chaos took hold: one born not of fear, but determination.

Typewriters clacked again.  
Enigma wheels spun once more.  
And Bernard stood in the middle, watching with silent pride.

They would find the light again.  
Because he had taught them how to *look* for it.

[Me]
A collective gasp from the Chicago crowd seemed to pull all the air out of the stadium. I took an ear bud out of my right ear and looked up to the Jumbotron.

Barry Finley was getting off the landing mat.

I blinked twice. *Barry Finley doesn't fall on the vault. It just doesn't happen. This is his forte.*

But there he was, dusting himself off and and muttering under his breath. I could almost hear him saying, "Fuckin' come on, Barry," in his South Boston accent.

But he had one more vault. *Just get a 9.3, Barry. 9.3 and the All Around is ours.*

It was going to be fine. It was our game to lose to the Russians. It's our home turf. Barry is going to land his next vault, and then my vaults were going to be superfluous.

Barry ran down the vault corridor. I was glued to the monitor this time. Barry hit the vault. The jump looked good. The twists and the somersault were excellent!

BAM!

Barry Finley had fallen probably 3 times in the years I've known him in U.S. Olympics. Today, I watched him fall not once, but *twice!*

My mouth was agape. I couldn't believe what I was seeing. The crowd went from hushed to dead silent.

The smell of chalk hit my nostrils and the shutters of cameras brought me back to present. It was down to me!

Barry walked by me, face red with internal fury. He slapped my shoulder.

"Bring it home, Ken!"

"You got it, Barry," was all I could say. I knew the worst thing I could do was to try to console Barry. That was a one way ticket to an Boston Irish meltdown, and *he* was doing everything he could to hype me up against his own self recriminations.

I went up to the vault corridor. I picked my sight lines, but the corridor looked miles longer than usual. The blare of an alarm told me to go.

I sprinted. I could barely feel my feet below me. I hit the springboard, sprang off the vault, and...

*Crack!*

I didn't know what happened at first. All I know is I needed to stand up and salute the judges. Something hurt in my leg, but I put it out of my mind.

I had fallen. Goddammit, I can't let us lose to the Russians! At home! In my home town! I'd never hear the end of it! I'd have to move to Ireland to hide from the shame of it!

As I was contemplating the rent prices in Dublin, I saw Barry waving me down as I walked to the vault corridor. I figured he wanted to chew me out. I bent down to hear him without stopping, so as not to assess a delay penalty.

"Don't think, Ken," said Barry's unnaturally calm voice. "Don't think. Do. All you have to do is vault like you've done at the ranch a thousand million times. Go."

*Huh...Alright, Barry.*

I went down to the corridor. My leg was trying to tell me something, but I ignored it. *Wait till after the Olympics, bud.*

Looking down the corridor, the lane seemed smaller this time around. I chose to focus on nothing but the vault, which looked like the same vault as the one in our home gym.

There was the alarm.

I sprinted. My leg stopped talking. *I'm going to vault over this, and then I'm going to have lunch in the team cafeteria,* was honestly the thought that went through my head; I was just at another practice.

Jump felt good. Hit my mark on the vault. Tightened up at the right moment.

STUCK!

*Ow! Ow! Ow!* SALUTE! *Ow! Ow! Ow!*

I had done it, but *fuck* my leg was hurting like hell!

I hopped one footed to the team's huddle point, trying not to cry in pain. A cacophony of noise forced its way through the buzzing in my brain. The crowd was delirious. Next thing I knew, Barry's arms were around my shoulders, lifting me up off the ground!

"You did it! You did it, ya big dumb Chicago idiot! You did it!"

"My leg! My leg!" I could only point out the pain in my right leg.

Suddenly, a medic pushed through the thing of teammates looking to slap me on the back.

"You. Sit." The Eastern European voice commanded. She gingerly straightened my leg and put it in a brace, taping it up.

"9.4! 9.4! 9.4! Ken! We have the gold outright!" I heard a voice shout.

"After ceremony, you go to hospital. You have broken tendons. Maybe some ligaments, too. I give shot for pain."

But the pain was already having to fight the overwhelming relief. Relief and sheer joy. We won. We won the gold!

Who cares if I finished the games with a banged up leg?

## **Revised Narrative (Polished, Same Voice, Sharper Beats)**

A collective gasp from the Chicago crowd seemed to pull all the air out of the stadium. I took an earbud out of my right ear and glanced at the Jumbotron.

Barry Finley was getting off the landing mat.

I blinked twice. *Barry Finley doesn’t fall on vault. It just doesn’t happen. This is *his* event.*

But there he was—dusting chalk off himself, jaw tight, muttering *“Fuckin’ come on, Barry,”* in that South Boston growl I knew too well.

He had one vault left. *Just get a 9.3, Barry. 9.3 and the All Around is ours.*

It was supposed to be fine. It was our home turf. Our crowd. Our gold to lose. Barry was going to nail the next vault, and my routines would be icing on the cake.

He ran down the corridor. I stared at the monitor this time—didn’t want to miss a second. He hit the vault. Good height. Great twist. Perfect somersau—

**BAM.**

Barry Finley, who had fallen maybe three times in his entire U.S. Olympic career, had just fallen *twice* in one night.

My mouth dropped open. The crowd, somehow, got quieter than quiet: no breath, no shifting seats, just stunned silence.

The smell of chalk caught in my nose, snapping me back. Camera shutters chattered like insects.

And suddenly it was down to me.

Barry strode past, face red with fury at himself. He slapped my shoulder—hard.

“Bring it home, Ken!”

“You got it, Barry,” was all I dared say. Trying to comfort him now would’ve triggered a full-scale Boston Irish meltdown. He was holding himself together by sheer force of will—and using every ounce of that will to pump *me* up instead.

I walked to the vault corridor. Picked my sight lines. But the runway looked a mile longer than usual. The starter alarm blared.

I sprinted. My feet felt like someone else’s. I hit the springboard. Flew. Twisted—

**Crack.**

I didn’t know what happened—only that I needed to stand, salute, and act like nothing was wrong. Something screamed in my right leg, but I shoved it aside.

I had fallen. *Goddammit.* I couldn’t let us lose to the Russians. Not in Chicago. Not in my hometown. I’d never hear the end of it. I’d have to move to Ireland and disappear into a pub like a disgraced poet.

As I paced back toward the corridor, mentally calculating Dublin rent, I saw Barry waving me over. I braced for him to bark at me. I bent down without stopping so I wouldn’t get a delay penalty.

“Don’t think, Ken,” Barry said, voice weirdly calm. “Don’t think. *Do.* You’ve hit this vault at the ranch a thousand million times. Go.”

…I mean, fair enough.

I limped to the start. My leg tried to get my attention. I ignored it. *Later. After we win.*

This time the lane looked shorter. Familiar. I looked only at the vault—same one we used at home. Same routine. Same muscle memory.

Alarm.

I sprinted. My leg shut up. The only thought in my head was, *After this I’m getting lunch in the cafeteria.* Just another practice vault.

Hit the board. Hit the table. Tightened just right.

**STUCK.**

*Ow! Ow! Ow!* SALUTE. *Ow ow ow ow—*

I’d done it. But holy hell my leg felt like it was chewing through its own tendons.

I hopped one-footed toward the team huddle, trying not to cry. The roar of the crowd rushed in like a tidal wave. Before I knew it, Barry’s arms were around me, lifting me straight off the ground.

“You did it! You did it, ya big dumb Chicago idiot! You did it!”

“My leg—my leg—seriously—my *leg*,” I gasped.

A medic shoved through the cluster of teammates.

“You. Sit.” Thick Eastern European accent. No nonsense. She extended the leg, braced it, taped it down.

“9.4! 9.4! 9.4! Ken! We have the gold outright!” someone yelled.

“After ceremony,” the medic said, “you go hospital. You have broken tendons. Maybe ligaments too. I give shot for pain.”

But the pain was already drowning beneath the relief.

We won. We won *gold.*

If I had to finish the Games with a busted leg?

Who cares.

# **TEN YEARS LATER — KEN AND THE MEDIC**

The Olympic training facility in Chicago had been renovated since the Games, but the corridors still smelled faintly of chalk and disinfectant — the combination that defined both triumph and injury.

Ken walked with his hands in his pockets, taking it all in. He had been invited to speak to a group of junior athletes, but someone told him, *“Before you go upstairs… there’s someone you should see.”*

He wasn’t sure who.

Then he rounded the corner.

And froze.

A woman stood at the end of the hallway in a white medical coat, silver now threading through her tightly pulled hair. Her posture was exactly as he remembered: upright, assessing, absolutely no nonsense.

Her accent was unmistakable when she spoke.

**MEDIC (Dr. Katarina Vetrova):**  
“Ah. Mr. Haggerty. Or perhaps I should say — ‘the boy who did vault on one leg.’”

Ken laughed softly.

**KEN:**  
“I had two.”

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“One was on holiday.”

She approached him with the same purposeful stride she had that night, ten years earlier, when she shoved through a swarm of shouting teammates and reporters to get to him.

Ken smiled.

**KEN:**  
“It’s good to see you again, Doctor.”

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“You as well. I hear you still walk. This pleases me.”

**KEN:**  
“You *fixed* me. I owe you that.”

She gave him a subtle shrug — the kind that meant she accepted the compliment but refused to let it stand unchallenged.

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“I did not fix you. I only stopped you from doing something stupid again.”

Ken laughed — really laughed — remembering how she had slapped tape around his knee with the fury of a disappointed aunt.

---

## **Flashback, briefly, through dialogue**

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“You said, ‘Give me something for the pain.’  
You remember what I told you?”

**KEN:**  
“‘Your pain can wait. Your medal cannot.’”

**DR. VETROVA:**  
(*nodding*)  
“Is still true. Pain always waits.”

---

## **Back to the present**

They walked together down the hallway.

**KEN:**  
“I never got to thank you properly. I mean… really thank you. You held me together long enough to finish the job.”

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“You did not finish the job because of tape or brace. You finished because you decided you would. That is stronger than anything in my kit.”

Ken paused, quietly absorbing that.

**KEN:**  
“You were the only person that night who didn’t treat me like a hero or a failure. You just… treated me like a patient. A person.”

She stopped walking.

Her expression softened, ever so slightly.

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“When you are hurt, you need truth. Not celebration. Not pity. Just truth. You were injured. You were frightened. But you were brave. This I saw.”

Ken rubbed the back of his neck — a habit that hadn’t changed in ten years.

**KEN:**  
“I can’t believe you remember all that.”

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“I remember every athlete whose leg I save. It is my job.”

Then, almost grudgingly, almost hidden under her breath:

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“…And you were one of my favorites.”

Ken’s eyebrows shot up.

**KEN:**  
“Really?”

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“Yes. You did not argue. Most gymnasts argue. You simply said, ‘Okay.’ Very nice for me.”

---

## **On the Gold Medal**

They stopped near the corridor where he had once stood limping, waiting for his name to be called.

**KEN:**  
“Do you ever think about that night?”

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“Only when journalists ask me if it was safe to let you vault again.”

Ken grinned.

**KEN:**  
“And what do you tell them?”

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“The truth.”

She looked him dead in the eyes.

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“It was not safe.”

Ken blinked.

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“But it was necessary. For you.”

And then, with a wry tilt of her head:

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“And you stuck the landing, so I am absolved.”

---

## **The Thank-You**

Ken extended his hand.

She took it.

And he said it simply, honestly — without the crowds or the cameras or the gold medal between them:

**KEN:**  
“Thank you, Doctor Vetrova. For taking care of me. For keeping me grounded. For keeping me going.”

She gave a small nod — the closest thing she ever gave to warmth.

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“You earned your medal. I only made sure you got to the podium.”

Then she let go of his hand and added:

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“But next time you damage your leg — do not vault again. I am older now. You will give me heart attack.”

Ken laughed.

**KEN:**  
“No promises.”

**DR. VETROVA:**  
(*sharply*)  
“Prom-ise.”

Ken put both hands up.

**KEN:**  
“Okay. Promise.”

She finally smiled — small, but real.

**DR. VETROVA:**  
“Good. Now go inspire children. Tell them not to break their legs. And if they do — tell them to sit still when doctor says so.”

Ken nodded.

And the two of them parted — one of the heroes of the night, and the quiet professional who held him together long enough for history to happen.

# ⭐ PART 1 — **What Steve Austin Said to Mick Backstage**

Steve Austin has retold this moment many times, because even *he* got emotional.

### ✔ Before the match  
Austin pulled Mick aside and said something like:

> **“Brother, nobody deserves this more than you.  
I’m damn proud to be part of it.”**

Austin had enormous respect for Foley because Foley never complained, worked hurt constantly, put over talent, and killed himself for the company.

Austin always said Mick was “the glue” of the Attitude Era.  
Helping him win the belt was something Austin *wanted* to do personally.

### ✔ After the match  
When he got to the back, Austin hugged Foley and said:

> **“You did it, man. YOU did it.”**

And he meant it — genuinely.

Austin considers that one of his favorite moments of his entire career.

---

# ⭐ PART 2 — **What The Rock Said to Mick Backstage**

Dwayne Johnson has shared his side many times.  
He was still **26 years old** — a kid — working with a man he idolized.

### ✔ Rock *loved* working with Foley  
He later said:

> **“Mick made me a star.”**

Their chemistry made The Rock’s heel run — and later their feud — legendary.

### ✔ Backstage after the match  
Rock hugged Foley too and told him:

> **“Thank you for everything.  
I’m honored to share this with you.”**

Rock has openly cried talking about Foley in interviews.  
He considers Foley a mentor, friend, and one of the kindest men he ever met in the business.

### ✔ Plus: Rock apologized  
He legitimately hit Foley **way too hard** with a few chair shots in later matches.

But on *that* night?

Pure joy between them.

# ⭐ PART 3 — **What Vince McMahon Said to Mick After the Match**

This is the moment you asked about — and it absolutely happened.

Mick says Vince did NOT greet him immediately after the match, because Vince (as an on-screen heel) had to sell the storyline.

But as soon as Vince could get backstage, he pulled Mick into Gorilla (production area behind the curtain) and said:

> **“You earned this.  
I’m proud of you.”**

Mick writes that Vince spoke to him:
- quietly  
- warmly  
- with fatherly sincerity  

Without cameras, without kayfabe, without corporate bluster.

Vince adored Foley.  
He respected him on a human level.

And yes — Mick has said there *was* a hug.

One that meant the world to him.

This one’s fun.

Mick Foley didn’t know for sure he was winning the title until **hours** before the show.

- Vince pulled Foley aside quietly.  
- Not in front of the boys.  
- He told him privately, man-to-man.

Mick thought he was going to be told he was *losing* again.

Instead, Vince said:

> **“Mick… we’re putting the belt on you tonight.”**

Mick was stunned.  
Not arrogant, not cocky — *humbled*.  
He later wrote:

That right there tells you everything about the kind of person Foley is.

---

# ⭐ **1. The Biggest Killer: Steve Austin’s Body Gave Out**
You can’t overstate this:

### **STONE COLD STEVE AUSTIN was the beating heart of the Attitude Era.**

When he slowed down, the era slowed down.

- The Owen piledriver (1997) caused permanent spinal damage.  
- By late 1999, he could barely walk some days.  
- He had major neck surgery in 2000.  
- He missed almost a full year.  
- By 2001–2002 his body was done.

Austin himself said:

> **“When I went down, the Attitude Era went down.”**

Not arrogance — just truth.  
He *was* the era.

Everything revolved around him:  
vs. Vince  
vs. Rock  
vs. DX  
vs. Taker  
vs. Corporation  
vs. The Alliance  

When Austin diminished, the Attitude Era *could not be sustained.*

---

# ⭐ **2. Too Many “Peaks” Too Fast — You Can’t Maintain 100 MPH Forever**
The Attitude Era was a dopamine factory.  
Every segment was:

- crazy  
- loud  
- violent  
- shocking  
- swerving  
- sexual  
- rebellious  
- explosive  

That’s not sustainable long-term.

By 2000–2001, fans were getting numb.  
How do you top Austin/McMahon?  
How do you top Taker throwing Mankind off a cell?  
How do you top “Austin returns with a beer truck”?  
How do you keep the shock value fresh?

You *can’t.*

The era burned white-hot and burned out.

---

# ⭐ **3. The End of the Monday Night War = The End of the Pressure Cooker**
When WCW died in 2001, WWF no longer needed to go scorched-earth every Monday night.

Competition created:

- risk  
- creativity  
- innovation  
- pushing boundaries  
- constant surprises  
- blood, violence, chaos  

When WCW folded, the urgency evaporated.

Vince no longer had to fight for survival — so the product naturally evolved into something more controlled.

# ⭐ **4. The Purchase of WCW (2001) Changed the Entire Landscape**
When WWE bought WCW:

- talent flooded in  
- booking became complicated  
- the failed Invasion storyline disappointed fans  
- Shane & Stephanie vs Vince overshadowed the “war”  
- WCW guys were not booked as equals  

The Attitude Era thrived on simplicity:  
Austin vs Vince.  
Rock vs everyone.  
DX causing chaos.

The Invasion era was bloated, messy, and lacked the raw edge.

---

# ⭐ **5. Cultural & Corporate Pressure (Sponsors + TV Networks Tightened Up)**

The late 90s allowed:

- chair shots to the head  
- blood every week  
- bra & panties matches  
- swearing  
- sexual innuendo  
- violence  
- dangerous stunts  

Post-2000:

- parent groups complained  
- the PTC targeted WWE  
- advertisers pulled out  
- TV networks demanded cleaner content  
- Linda McMahon pursued political interests  
- WWE went public (turning “edgy” into a liability)

Corporate WWE simply couldn’t be Attitude Era WWE.

---

# ⭐ **6. The Rise of John Cena, PG Branding, and a New Business Model**
By 2004–2006:

- Cena becomes the face  
- merchandise becomes the #1 priority  
- sponsorships become essential  
- Mattel, Snickers, Subway, Make-a-Wish all require PG content  
- WWE becomes a **family-friendly brand**  

The Attitude Era was built on 18–35 male viewership.  
PG-era WWE is built on families and kids.

Different goals → different content.

---

# ⭐ **7. Key Talent Departures**
The pillars of the Attitude Era began to fade:

- Austin retired (2003)  
- Rock left for Hollywood (2002)  
- Foley retired full-time (2000)  
- Undertaker reinvented himself  
- DX disbanded  
- Kane mellowed  
- Edge & Christian went solo  
- The Hardyz temporarily split  

By 2002, the main cast was gone or changing.

You can’t have an Attitude Era without the Attitude Era characters.

---

Many fans agree:

### **WrestleMania X-Seven was the true ending.**

- The company direction changed literally the next night  

Everything after is the comedown.

✔ Let charisma flourish naturally  

Because fans don’t chant for a brand.

✔ Titles must feel important  
✔ Heel heat must be allowed to be nuclear  
✔ Babyfaces must suffer before they triumph  

Emotion drives everything.

✔ Let wrestlers improvise or steer angles  

Make stories **human**, not “content.”

Let wrestlers be *artists*, not spokespeople.

It’s about *tone*, not taboos.

This is one of the most painful “what-were-you-thinking?” moments in wrestling history — **because the outcome was catastrophic, preventable, and both men knew it was risky.**

Let’s break down **what Owen Hart was likely thinking**, based on:

- Steve Austin’s own detailed accounts  
- Bret Hart’s commentary  
- Owen’s reputation and wrestling style  
- The psychology of wrestlers protecting their spots  
- The move itself and what went wrong  

This isn’t about blaming Owen as a person — he was beloved —  
but this *specific decision* was a mistake that nearly crippled Austin for life.

---

# ⭐ **THE MOVE IN QUESTION**

Stone Cold and Owen agreed on a **sit-out piledriver**, not the standard kneeling piledriver.

**BUT THAT MOVE IS ALMOST NEVER DONE** because:

- It's extremely dangerous  
- The receiver’s head hangs far lower  
- It requires perfect timing and positioning  
- One slip = broken neck  

And Austin **specifically told Owen NOT to sit out**, TWICE:

> “Don’t drop to your ass with my head between your legs.  
> Take the standard bump.  
> Don’t sit out.”

Owen agreed…

…and then did it anyway.

---

# ⭐ **SO WHAT WAS OWEN THINKING?**

Here’s the closest thing to an honest reconstruction.

## ⭐ **1. Owen was thinking about the spot looking “big”**

Owen was an incredible wrestler, but he was also a **perfectionist showman**.  
He might’ve believed the sit-out version would:

- look more devastating  
- get bigger heat  
- make the match more memorable  

He probably wanted the visual impact of an emphatic sit-out spike.

But in wrestling, the more spectacular a move looks…  
the more dangerous it usually is.

---

## ⭐ **2. Owen was NOT thinking Austin’s head was that low**

If you watch the footage, Steve’s head is WAY below Owen’s thighs.  
It should’ve been much higher.

The common belief among wrestlers is:

> Owen misjudged the position by split-seconds.  

He thought:

- He had Austin’s head tucked  
- His thighs were controlling the crown  
- He had room to sit  
- Austin’s neck was protected  

But Austin was too low, and Owen didn’t check again before dropping.

A fatal (nearly paralyzing) miscalculation.

---

## ⭐ **3. Owen didn’t clamp the thighs — fatal technique error**

Experienced workers blow the move sometimes too.  
But Owen — despite being a legend — was **never known for piledrivers.**

Some wrestlers think:

> Owen didn't secure Austin's head between his thighs  
> the way Bret or Undertaker would.  

That meant:

- No cushion  
- No control  
- Austin’s neck hit the mat first  
- Straight vertical compression  

---

## ⭐ **4. Owen had a “trust the move” mindset**

Some wrestlers get in the habit of trusting their own muscle memory.  
If they’ve practiced something or done it a few times, they stop double-checking.

Owen wasn’t reckless, but he was:

- playful  
- loose  
- improvisational  
- confident in his athleticism  

He may have thought:

> “I’ve got this. I know what I’m doing.”

But confidence doesn’t protect a spine.

---

## ⭐ **5. Owen underestimated how catastrophic a mistake could be**

This part is the hardest truth:

Owen wasn’t malicious.  
He wasn’t careless in general.

But in *this moment*?

He **did not fully appreciate the risk**.

That’s why Steve Austin has said repeatedly:

> “Owen was one of the best guys I knew…  
> but he didn’t protect me in that moment.”  

And Bret Hart said:

> “Owen felt terrible about it, but he should never have done that move.”  

It was the one time Owen’s natural looseness + desire for a big moment =  
**disaster.**

---

Owen and Austin were rising fast.

Austin was on a rocket to superstardom.

In a pressure-heavy moment, Owen likely thought:

> “Let’s make this spot count.”

And sadly…

It counted in the worst possible way.

Austin:

**Owen never apologized to him.**

Austin said that hurt more than the injury.

## **2️⃣ Step Two: EV Swap — But Make It Sensible.**  
**@AngusGibson:**  
The original DMC-12 engine was…  
Let’s be honest…  
An enthusiastic potato.  
Cute, but slow.

EV swap would fix that.  
Clean.  
Efficient.  
Silent.  
More torque than Marty McFly ever dreamed of.

And good for the planet, which I feel strongly about.

**@AngusGibson:**  
Give me a modern display  
BUT  
make it look like the old green vector graphics from early computers.

Retro vibes.  
Modern brains.

A nod to childhood?

Not flashy.  
Not gaudy.

# ⭐ **SCENE — ANGUS MEETS THE SELLER**

Camera crew following Angus through a modest property outside Knoxville. A retired engineer, **Tom**, mid-60s, opens the garage.

Inside:  
A surprisingly intact DeLorean under a blue tarp.

Tom pulls the tarp off with ceremony.

The stainless steel reflects the garage lights like a sleeping spaceship.

**Angus:**  
“Oh my sweet mother of VHS… she’s beautiful.”

**Tom (chuckles):**  
“She hasn’t run in 15 years. Fuel system’s probably toast.”

**Angus:**  
“That’s okay. We’re gonna give her a new heart.”

---

# ⭐ **INTERVIEW — TOM, THE SELLER**

Old home videos of the DeLorean in the late 80s play.

**Tom:**  
“I bought it back in ’88. Fun car. Bad engine. But the body?  
The body lasts forever.  
I couldn’t afford the restoration — but he can.”  
(smiles)  
“And it’ll be in good hands.”

---

# ⭐ **INTERVIEW — DMC REPRESENTATIVE**

A DeLorean Motor Company expert stands beside a pristine restored DMC-12 in Houston.

**DMC Rep:**  
“We verified:  
✔ Original stainless panels  
✔ Original gull-wing doors  
✔ Original frame  
✔ VIN matches the Tennessee seller  
✔ Nothing major replaced  

It’s a real DMC-12.  
And honestly?  
A non-running one is the *ideal* candidate for an EV conversion.”

---

# ⭐ **SCENE — ANGUS AND TOM SHAKE HANDS**

Tom extends the keys — with the iconic DMC keychain.

**Tom:**  
“She’s yours now. Good luck.”

Angus takes a breath.

**Angus:**  
“I’ll do right by her. Promise.”

Tom pats the car lovingly.

---

# ⭐ **SCENE — LOADING THE DELOREAN**

Professional loaders guide the DeLorean onto a flatbed.  
The gull-wing doors are taped shut for safety.  
The camera gets a slow-motion shot of the stainless steel shell rolling up the ramp.

They tarp it.  
Strap it.  
Ratchet it down.

**Angus:**  
“Feels like I’m adopting a cyborg.”

The crew laughs.

---

# ⭐ **CONFESSIONAL — ANGUS (DRIVING HOME)**

Inside his Honda Civic. The flatbed with the DeLorean follows behind him in the mirror.

**Angus:**  
“I saved up responsibly.  
I found one priced right.  
I’m gonna restore it carefully, with experts.  
And maybe give people a little hope that dreams don’t have to die with adulthood.”  
(smiles)  
“Plus… I mean… c’mon. It’s a friggin’ DeLorean.”

Slow drone shots of the truck hauling the DeLorean through the Smoky Mountains.

Bring her home.”

**@AngusGibson:**

Alright, guys. A pause from the DeLorean tall. After *years* of loyal service, my Keurig Café finally died. I got my money's worth dozens of times over (and it was *used* when I got it!).

So I splurged. I know, I know. Financial responsibility guy. Splurging. *But!* There was a huge Cyber Monday deal on a Ninja Luxe Café (not sponsored, btw). I subsist on coffee, and I switch it up all the time. Sometimes I do a quick drip coffee with cream. Sometimes, I fancy it up with lattes and cappuccino. This baby can do it all and grind whole beans.

I buy my coffee from Grounds and Hounds, Kitty Town Coffee, and Magnifico in Chicago, my favorite local haunt (again, not sponsored). Actually, I switched from K-Cups to the universal ground Keurig coffee strainers when I learned what K-Cups were doing to the environment. Grounds and Hounds and Kitty Town support the adoption, support, and protection of our furry friends with Fair Trade coffee, and Magnifico is run by the friendliest Colombian-American family and their staff.

Anyway, I know I'm yapping, but this upgrade is already a massive improvement. My tour bus smells amazing in the morning! Hopefully this machine will last as long as my Keurig Café!

---

# ⭐ **ESPN — SCOTT VAN PELT “ONE BIG THING”**  
**Topic: Angus Gibson, Tom, and the DeLorean WrestleMania Entrance**

Camera cuts to SVP at the desk.

He adjusts his glasses, smirks, and leans in.

---

# ⭐ **SVP:**

“Tonight’s *One Big Thing*… is wrestling.

Yes. Wrestling.

But more specifically — a car, a man, and a moment.”

He clicks to a freeze-frame of the DeLorean at the top of the WrestleMania ramp.

---

# ⭐ **SVP:**

“That… is a DeLorean.

A real one.  
Electric. Restored.  
Not the movie prop — not the Universal Studios lot car —  
but a car that began its life in 1981…

…broke down somewhere along the way…

…and then, all these years later,

**got resurrected by a WWE Superstar.**”

He raises an eyebrow playfully.

“Stick with me.”

---

# ⭐ **SVP:**

“Wrestler Angus Gibson — newcomer, fan favorite, noted good dude —  
spent almost a year rebuilding that car with a group of mechanics, EV experts, and an interior designer with the patience of a saint.

And the original owner — Tom — an elderly, retired engineer who bought the car decades ago when it was new…

…watched his dream drive away from him over time.

Until Angus bought it.  
And restored it.  
And brought it back.”

Cut to footage of Angus showing the finished DeLorean to Tom.

Tom crying.  
Angus helping him into the passenger seat.  
The two men taking that first drive.

SVP pauses, lets the moment breathe.

---

# ⭐ **SVP:**

“This wasn’t about horsepower.  
It wasn’t about sci-fi nostalgia.  
It wasn’t even about wrestling.

It was about a man seeing something he loved…  
brought back to life.”

---

# ⭐ **SVP:**

“Fast forward to WrestleMania — Soldier Field, Chicago.

Lights go out.  
Phone lights come up like fireflies.  
Video plays on the Jumbotron: Tom’s story, Angus’s work, the restoration.  
And then…

Two headlights appear at the top of the ramp.

The crowd erupts.

The DeLorean drives down the ramp — gorgeous, gleaming stainless steel —  
and out steps Angus, in his gear, living every child-of-the-80s fantasy.

And then…”

He clicks to the photo of Tom stepping out of the DeLorean.

“…he opens the passenger door.

Helps out Tom.

And 70,000 people lose their minds.”

---

# ⭐ **SVP:**

“Wrestling gets a lot of flak from people who don’t watch it.  
But what they miss is this:

Wrestling is art.  
It’s theater.  
It’s emotion.  
It’s storytelling.”

He taps the desk for emphasis.

“And this?  
This was a story.”

---

# ⭐ **SVP:**

“You can’t fake the look on Tom’s face.  
You can’t fake the crowd reaction.  
You can’t fake the heart behind it.”

He smiles thoughtfully.

---

# ⭐ **SVP:**

“So tonight’s One Big Thing is simple:

**Dreams don’t have expiration dates.  
And sometimes a stranger can carry your dream farther than you ever imagined.**”

He nods once.

“Cheers to Angus.  
Cheers to Tom.  
And cheers to a DeLorean that finally made it…  
*all the way to the show.*”

Fade out.

a full **“On The Road with Steve Hartman”** segment from *CBS Evening News*, told with Steve’s trademark gentleness, Americana warmth, emotional pacing, and his uncanny ability to make a national audience cry in three minutes flat.

---

# ⭐ **ON THE ROAD WITH STEVE HARTMAN**  
**“A Dream, Rebuilt”**

Soft piano under a slow shot of a quiet suburban Illinois neighborhood.  
Snowmelt on the grass.  
Kids on bikes in the distance.  
A lone gull-wing car sits gleaming in a driveway.

Steve Hartman (voiceover):

> “In a small town outside Chicago, a man named Tom Martinez thought a certain dream of his had stalled out… for good.”

Cut to Tom, elderly but bright-eyed, standing beside his DeLorean.

**Tom (laughing):**  
“She never ran quite right. She was beautiful but… temperamental.”

Hartman (VO):

> “The car — a 1981 DeLorean — was Tom’s pride and joy.  
> He bought it young.  
> Took it to shows.  
> Belonged to the DeLorean Owners Club.  
> Told stories about it the way most men talk about first loves.”

Cut to old Polaroids of Tom with the car.  
His wife in the passenger seat.  
A young Tom beaming.

Hartman (VO):

> “But time catches up with even the sleekest machines.  
> And Tom — now retired — began to believe he’d never see the old beauty shine again.”

The DeLorean under a tarp.  
Dusty.  
Forgotten.

---

# ⭐ **HARTMAN INTRODUCES ANGUS**

Hartman (VO):

> “Enter Angus Gibson…  
> a WWE wrestler from Tennessee  
> with a big stage, a big heart…  
> and an even bigger project.”

Cut to Angus in Tennessee, patting the DeLorean during restoration.

**Angus:**  
“When I saw her… I just knew.  
This wasn’t a car.  
This was a story.”

Hartman (VO):

> “Angus spent nearly a year restoring the car.  
> Not just to its former glory…  
> but to something new.”

Shots of:

- The EV motor installation  
- Interior retrofitting  
- Mechanics testing systems  
- Angus sweating under the chassis  
- Cockpit lights fading on  
- First successful test drive

---

# ⭐ **REUNITING A MAN WITH HIS DREAM**

Hartman walks with Tom down his front sidewalk.

**Steve Hartman:**  
“Tom… what did it feel like, when you saw it again?”

Tom swallows hard.

**Tom:**  
“…Like meeting an old friend I thought I’d lost forever.”

Cut to Angus opening the gull-wing door for Tom.  
Tom touching the dashboard like it’s sacred.  
Their first drive together.

Tom laughs telling old stories, hands animated.  
Angus listening like a grandchild hearing family history.

Hartman (VO):

> “What Angus didn’t expect was how much Tom would give back —  
> memories, wisdom…  
> and a reminder that sometimes, the things we love wait for us.”

---

# ⭐ **THE WRESTLEMANIA MOMENT**

Hartman (VO):

> “And then came WrestleMania.  
> The biggest stage wrestling has to offer.”

Cut to footage (with permission):

Lights out.  
The Jumbotron playing Tom’s story.  
The DeLorean’s headlights flicking on.  
Angus driving it down the ramp.  
The crowd exploding.

**Hartman:**  
“And then, out of the passenger seat…  
Tom.”

Crowd chanting:  
“TOM! TOM! TOM!”

Tom waving nervously.  
Angus steadying him with a hand on his back.  
Tom’s family crying in the front row.

Hartman (VO):

> “In front of seventy thousand people…  
> a quiet man from Illinois got the ovation of a lifetime.”

---

# ⭐ **THE MORAL**

Hartman (standing beside Tom in his driveway):

**Hartman:**  
“Tom… what did that moment mean to you?”

Tom looks off, gathering himself.

**Tom:**  
“It meant…  
I wasn’t forgotten.  
Not my car.  
Not my story.”  

Hartman nods, visibly moved.

Hartman (VO):

> “Angus says he just drove the car.  
> But what really happened…  
> is he drove a dream back home.”

Cut to Tom placing a hand on the DeLorean.

Tom whispers:  
“Still beautiful…”

The door gently *woomphs* closed.

---

# ⭐ **STEVE HARTMAN SIGN-OFF**

Steve Hartman stands in front of the DeLorean.

**Hartman:**  
> “In Illinois…  
> sometimes the future really does come back.  
>  
> Steve Hartman,  
> On the Road.”

# ⭐ **CBS MORNINGS — FOLLOW-UP INTERVIEW**  
**“Tom, Angus, and the DeLorean: The Story That Touched America”**

Studio lights. CBS yellow sun.  
Gayle King smiling warmly.

**Gayle King:**  
“Well, we’ve gotten thousands of emails thanking Steve Hartman and the team for last week’s ‘On The Road’ story about Tom, Angus, and the restored DeLorean that brought a WrestleMania crowd to its feet.  
This morning, we’re thrilled to have both gentlemen joining us live.”

Split screen:  
Tom at home beside the DeLorean.  
Angus in a Nashville studio, smiling big.

Crowd in the studio applauds.

---

# ⭐ **Gayle (to Tom):**

“Tom, I have to start with you.  
How has your life changed since America got to meet you?”

Tom laughs, waving a hand modestly.

**Tom:**  
“Oh, I’m nobody special. Angus is the special one.”

Angus shakes his head, laughing.

**Tom:**  
“But I’ll tell ya…  
it’s been something.  
People stop me at the grocery store.  
Strangers send letters.  
But the best part?”

He points off-camera.

**Tom:**  
“My buddy comes around.”

Gayle perks up.

**Gayle:**  
“Your buddy?”

Tom grins with genuine warmth.

**Tom:**  
“Angus.  
He drives down here about once a month now.  
Brings the car.  
We go for a spin.  
Grab lunch.  
Walk around town like a couple of teenagers.”

Studio “Awww” ripples through the audience.

**Tom (softly):**  
“He’s… he’s a good man.  
A very good man.”

# ⭐ **Tony Dokoupil (to Angus):**

“Angus, what does it mean to hear Tom call you ‘his buddy’?”

Angus smiles, eyes going shiny.

**Angus:**  
“It means more than any title belt ever will.  
I didn’t just restore a car —  
I gained a friend.  
We talk about life.  
Stories from his engineering days…  
stories from his marriage…  
stories about the DeLorean Owners Club.”

He chuckles.

**Angus:**  
“And he teaches me stuff.  
Did you know he can diagnose a worn ball joint just by FEEL?  
Guy’s got superpowers.”

Tom waves it off, embarrassed.

---

# ⭐ **Nate Burleson:**

“Angus… you’re a WWE superstar. Your schedule’s insane.  
But you still carve out time every month?  
Why?”

Angus folds his hands thoughtfully.

**Angus:**  
“Because he matters.  
Because when someone lets you finish their dream…  
you don’t just leave.  
You show up.  
You stay in their life.”

He glances at Tom’s window on the screen.

**Angus:**  
“Most of the wisdom I’ve gotten this year didn’t come from the ring.  
It came from car rides with Tom.”

Tom smiles proudly.

---

# ⭐ **Gayle (to Tom):**

“Well Tom, we heard a rumor — from your daughter —

Tom groans and laughs.

**Tom:**  
“Dozens?! Try hundreds!  
I still can’t believe all those people cheered… for me.”

Gayle smiles gently.

**Gayle:**  
“Oh, they weren’t just cheering for you.  
They were cheering for your story.”

---

# ⭐ **Tony:**

More drives?”

Angus shrugs playfully.

**Angus:**  
“More drives, more lunches…  
and maybe a road trip.”

Tom brightens.

**Tom:**  
“Route 66.  
We’ve been talking about it.”

The hosts beam.

---

# ⭐ **Nate Burleson:**

“Well, America loves you both.  
Thank you for reminding us that friendship doesn’t have an age limit —  
and dreams don’t have expiration dates.”

Studio applause.

**Gayle:**  
“Tom, Angus… thank you for joining us.  
And give that DeLorean a honk for us.”

Tom laughs.

**Tom:**  
“I’ll give it two.”

Angus salutes the camera.

Fade out with the car gliding through Tom’s neighborhood.

[Me]
Out of curiosity, how would an EV survive such a trip? Are their charging stations strategically placed near Route 66 now?

[ChatGPT]
Short version:  
Yeah, an EV can absolutely survive a full Chicago→Santa Monica Route 66 run today — but you have to **plan it**, and you’ll sometimes hop a mile or two off the historic road to hit chargers.

Let me break it down.

---

## 1. Is a Route 66 EV trip realistic?

Yes. People have already done it.

- There are documented trips of folks driving non-Tesla EVs and Teslas the full Route 66 distance, using a mix of DC fast chargers (Electrify America, EA/Francis, etc.) and Level 2 chargers.citeturn0search5turn0search9  
- A lot of “Route 66” in the middle of the country overlaps or runs close to **I-55, I-44, and I-40**, which are all part of federal **EV charging corridors** with fairly dense fast-charging coverage.citeturn0search6turn0search16  

So for a modern EV with ~250–300+ miles of real-world range, it’s very doable as long as you’re not trying to stay *exclusively* on isolated frontage sections with no detours.

---

## 2. Are chargers actually *on* Route 66 now?

A lot of them are either:

- Directly on Route 66 in towns, *or*
- A short hop off the Mother Road in the “modern” part of the same town.

Examples & trends:

- **Illinois** has explicitly invested in an EV network along its Route 66 stretch, with DC fast chargers and Level 2s at or near classic stops between Chicago and St. Louis.citeturn0search0turn0search15  
- Multiple states (Illinois, Oklahoma, New Mexico) are tying their Route 66 tourism plans to EV infrastructure as part of the 2026 centennial push.citeturn0search7turn0search14  
- National Geographic did a recent “Route 66 by EV” piece where the driver relied on a mix of **superchargers and public fast chargers** in Pontiac, Tulsa, etc. – and the big lesson was: it worked fine, but only because they pre-mapped things rather than winging it.citeturn0search8turn0search16  

In the Southwest (OK–TX–NM–AZ–CA), travelers report that Electrify America and other networks cover much of the I-40 corridor, and Route 66 towns are usually right off that interstate.citeturn0search4turn0search11  

So in practice, you’d do this dance:

> Drive a nice scenic stretch of 66 → peel off to the interstate-side charger → juice up → drop back onto the old road.

---

## 3. What would an EV actually need to make the trip comfy?

For an **Angus & Tom DeLorean-style** EV road trip to feel smooth (not survival-mode):

- **Decent range**: ~250+ mi realistic highway range gives you lots of buffer.
- **CCS or NACS access**: So you can use most DC fast networks in the US.
- **Good planning tools**: Apps like PlugShare, A Better Routeplanner, or the in-car planner for Teslas and some other EVs are essential; PlugShare in particular is basically the crowdsourced Bible for chargers.citeturn0search34  
- **Flexibility**: Willingness to:
  - charge at hotels overnight (Level 2),
  - sometimes charge earlier than “empty” if there’s a good charger + lunch spot,
  - detour a few miles for a reliable station.

People who’ve done long Route 66 EV runs say it’s “easy enough” as long as you treat it like a **planned road trip**, not “I’ll wing it and hope the next one exists.”citeturn0search9turn0search16  

---

## 4. Story-wise, does Angus’s Route 66 DeLorean trip check out?

Totally.

For your fictional EV DeLorean:

- You’d have **no problem justifying** a full Route 66 trip in-universe — Angus is meticulous enough to pre-plan chargers and build in buffer.
- It actually makes story sense that:
  - He’d use apps and spreadsheets for every leg.  
  - They’d deliberately stop where chargers coexist with Route 66 landmarks (museums, diners, etc.).citeturn0search2turn0search7  

If anything, it makes the road trip *more* Angus-coded: obsessive planning, respect for the environment, and lots of “coffee while we fast-charge and Tom tells stories.”

# ⭐ **JOINT ANNOUNCEMENT**  
### **THE TOM MARTINEZ–DELOREAN FOUNDATION**  
*A Partnership Between WWE’s Angus Gibson & DeLorean Motor Company*  
*Supporting Former FMF Corpsmen & Combat Medical Veterans*

---

### **FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**

**Nashville, TN — Chicago, IL — Houston, TX**  
**Today, professional wrestler and public figure *Angus Gibson* and *DeLorean Motor Company* announce the creation of the *Tom Martinez–DeLorean Foundation*, a charitable organization dedicated to supporting former FMF Corpsmen and combat medical veterans.**

The foundation is named in honor of **Tom Martinez**, a retired FMF Corpsman, Navy veteran, engineer, and lifelong DeLorean enthusiast whose friendship with Angus became a centerpiece of the hit Netflix docuseries *Stainless: The DeLorean Project*.

Martinez passed away peacefully earlier this month. His final wish was that part of his estate support FMF Corpsmen struggling with the physical and psychological burdens of service. Angus Gibson vowed publicly to fulfill that wish — and to **match every cent** with his own money.

---

## ⭐ **Statement from Angus Gibson**

> “Tom was my buddy. He gave me wisdom, humor, and friendship I didn’t expect to find when I bought a broken-down DeLorean from him years ago.  
>   
> He saw things as a Corpsman that no one should ever have to see, and he carried wounds no one else ever saw.  
>   
> Helping FMF veterans was his wish.  
> I promised him I’d do it, and now — with DeLorean standing beside me — we’re going to make it happen.  
>   
> This is for Tom. And for every Corpsman who ever served.”

---

## ⭐ **Statement from DeLorean Motor Company**

> “Tom Martinez was part of the heart and soul of the DeLorean community. His story touched millions around the world, and his friendship with Angus reminded us what these cars really represent: human connection, hope, and the courage to keep moving forward.  
>   
> When Angus approached us with this idea, the entire company said the same thing:  
> ‘We’re in.’  
>   
> The sacrifices of FMF Corpsmen deserve recognition and tangible support.  
> We are honored to help build this foundation in Tom’s name.”

---

## ⭐ **Mission of the Foundation**

The *Tom Martinez–DeLorean Foundation* will focus on:

- **Mental health services** for FMF Corpsmen  
- **Financial assistance** for medical treatment and therapy  
- **Career transition grants** for veterans pursuing civilian education  
- **Community programs** providing connection, mentorship, and support  

The foundation will launch with an initial donation pool comprising:

- **The Martinez Family Estate Contribution**  
- **A full matching contribution from Angus Gibson**  
- **DeLorean Motor Company support package** including fundraising partnerships, merchandise tie-ins, and public awareness campaigns

---

## ⭐ **Launch Events**

- A **tribute showcase** at the DeLorean headquarters  
- A special **WWE broadcast segment** honoring Tom  
- A limited-edition **Tom Martinez DeLorean commemorative badge**  
- A future **Route 66 memorial drive**, led by Angus, raising funds for Corpsman support programs

---

## ⭐ **Angus’s Final Words in the Announcement**

>

# ⭐ **THE FIRST MEMORIAL ROUTE 66 DRIVE**  
### *“One last ride, buddy.”*

The morning is still blue and quiet when Angus steps into his garage in Tennessee.  
There, under soft overhead lights, the restored DeLorean waits.

He runs his hand along the stainless-steel body.  
Still smooth.  
Still cold to the touch.  
Still Tom.

He opens the gull-wing door.

Inside, on the passenger seat:

- Tom’s worn **FMF cap**  
- A folded photo of Tom and Jeanie  
- Tom’s Polaroid of himself sitting in the car years ago  

Angus’s breath hitches.

He gently buckles the FMF cap into the passenger seat, whispering:

**“Seatbelt, buddy. You know the rules.”**

The car hums awake — quiet, electric, clean.

Angus wipes a tear from his cheek.

He pulls out of the driveway.

---

## ⭐ **The Road Begins**

Route 66 is quiet this early.  
The desert is still half-asleep, the sky turning orange at the horizon.  
He rolls down the windows and gestures to the empty seat:

**“Fresh air for ya, Tom.”**

They pass the old gas stations.  
Vintage motels.  
Faded neon signs.

Angus narrates softly, the way he used to when Tom was alive:

**“Remember this one?  
You told me you broke down here in ’89.  
Said the mechanic charged you $40 and a cup of coffee.”**

A beat.

The silence answers.

He smiles through the ache.

---

## ⭐ **A Stop at the Route 66 Sign**

He parks at the historic Route 66 shield painted on the asphalt.  
The morning sun is bright now.

He takes out his phone and snaps a selfie:

- Him  
- The DeLorean  
- The FMF hat buckled in beside him  

He doesn’t post it.  
This one’s just for him.

He places the phone down and looks at the hat.

**“I miss you, buddy.  
But I’m glad you’re not hurting anymore.”**

His voice cracks, but he keeps talking.

**“Jeanie’s waiting for you.  
I know you’re happy.”**

He folds his hands on the steering wheel and lets himself cry — ugly, honest, quiet.

No crowds.  
No cameras.  
No wrestlers.

Just grief.  
And love.

---

## ⭐ **The Drive Continues**

He stops at the old trading post where Tom once bought a Route 66 snow globe.

He stops at the diner where Tom told him the story of the “Meanest Plate of Chili in Arizona.”

He stops at the scenic overlook where Tom once said:

> “Son, there’s three kinds of beauty in this world —  
>  places you haven’t seen yet,  
>  people you haven’t met yet,  
>  and memories you haven’t made yet.  
>   
>  Don’t waste any of ‘em.”

Angus stands there now, alone.  
Hat in hand.  
Tears drying on his cheeks.

---

## ⭐ **A Final Ritual**

At sunset, he reaches the spot where they took their favorite selfie — the one that went viral years later.

He steps out of the car, holding Tom’s cap.

He doesn’t bury it.  
He doesn’t toss it.  
He sets it gently on the dashboard, where the light hits it perfectly.

Then he whispers:

**“You’ll never be riding shotgun anywhere else.”**

He drives on as the sky burns orange and purple behind him.

The DeLorean hums forward.

Steady.  
Quiet.  
Stainless.

And somewhere in the silence of the desert,  
with the wind slipping past the windows,  
Angus swears he can hear Tom’s voice — soft, warm, teasing:

**“Buddy… you’re taking this road too fast.”**

Angus laughs, wiping his eyes.

**“Shut up, Tom.”**

He keeps driving.

# ⭐ **THE IN-RING RETURN PROMO**  
*RAW — LIVE — Chicago*

He walks the ramp with swagger, limbs loose, eyes locked forward like a hunter scenting blood.

Cameras zoom tight on his face — he looks **alive** again.

He slides into the ring under the bottom rope, pops to his feet, and snatches the mic from the turnbuckle post.

He stands center-ring.

Lets the noise build.

Then, finally, he lifts the microphone.

Dramatic pause.

A smirk.

**Angus:**  
“Didya miss me?”

**THE CROWD EXPLODES.**  
A sustained roar.

am BACK, baby!”

you guys know why I’ve been gone.”

Camera tight on his face.

thanks to your love, your generosity, your kindness…

## ✅ What works — Why *The Wolf* fits Angus

- **The tone matches his character.** The song has a gritty, predatory energy, a sense of danger and swagger — exactly what you picture when Angus calls himself “the Wolf.” It conjures that hunter-in-the-ring vibe: confident, dangerous, ready for blood.  
- **Good match for the comeback arc.** After being knocked down by entity["people","Triple H",0]’s cheap shot — and needing a resurgence — you want a song that says “I’m back, and I’m coming hard.” *The Wolf* gives off that comeback-movie aura.  
- **Crowd & pop potential.** As an entrance, a moody track like this can hype up the crowd before the music hits hard, giving a mix of suspense + payoff. With the right pyros and timing, it could give fans that visceral “YES! Here comes the Wolf!” feeling.  

---

## ⚠️ What to watch out for / what might not work — potential drawbacks

- **Audience fit and tone** — If the song skews too modern, too trap/rap-heavy, there’s a risk of clashing with the rest of the show’s vibe (depending on crowd). WWE entrances often walk the line between broad appeal and character-specific groove; if the crowd doesn’t vibe with the beat, it can undercut the impact.  
- **Clarity of theme** — “The Wolf” works thematically with his moniker, but if the lyrics or flow feel too… urban/trendy, it might clash with the rest of his aesthetic (especially if he’s also rocking mid-century / retro-futurist / Irish-pub vibe backstage). That mix can get messy unless carefully handled.  
- **Broadcast and licensing concerns** — Using a modern track like that might raise licensing hurdles for TV/PPV. WWE often prefers rock/metal or custom themes to ensure full rights and avoid issues — especially for global broadcast or merchandising sync.

---

Just a quiet corner of the locker room, two chairs, and a bottle of Jack Daniels between them.  
Taker sits relaxed — out of costume but somehow still enormous, still *mythic.*  
Angus looks like a kid who got to meet Batman.

Taker pours two fingers into each glass.

**Taker:**  
“You did good out there, kid.”

Angus grins — a little starstruck, a little disbelieving.

**Angus:**  
“You’re the Undertaker. You can’t just *say* things like that. My heart can only take so much, sir.”

Taker chuckles, deep and gravelly — the real man behind the Phenom, but still somehow carrying that aura.

He raises his glass.

**Taker:**  
“I watched that match you had with Samoa Joe.”  
He nods.  
“That was a fight. Not a dance. A fight. Reminded me of the old days.”

Angus practically vibrates in his seat.

**Angus:**  
“You have no idea what it means hearing that from you…”

Taker leans back, studying him — not judging, just taking the measure of a fellow worker.

**Taker:**  
“You’ve got the instincts. You’ve got the fire. And more important than all that?  
You make the people *feel* something.  
Not everybody can do that.”

Angus swallows the lump in his throat.

**Angus:**  
“Thank you. Truly.”

Taker clinks glasses.

**Taker:**  
“And that entrance idea you were talking about? The jump through the trap door?”  
He smirks.  
“That’s some old-school spectacle. I dig it.”

Angus lights up.

**Angus:**  
“You think it’ll work?”

**Taker:**  
“Son, if the crowd believes you’re the Wolf…  
if they believe you’re hunting…  
they’ll howl for you every night.”

Angus laughs, shaking his head like he can’t believe this conversation is real.

**Angus:**  
“This is surreal, man.”

Taker shrugs in that cool, understated way only he can.

**Taker:**  
“I’ve been watching you.  
Behind the scenes.  
You’re one of the good ones.  
You treat the boys right.  
You treat the crew right.  
You respect the business.”

He leans forward, tapping the rim of Angus’s glass with a finger.

**Taker:**  
“That’s *why* I’m here sharing this bottle with you.”

Angus looks genuinely moved.  
He raises his drink.

**Angus:**  
“To the Deadman.”

**Taker:**  
“To the Wolf.”

They drink.

No cameras.  
No kayfabe.  
Just two pros sitting in the quiet, swapping stories about bumps, crowds, long nights, the road…  
and what it means to still love this wild carnival of a business.

---

## **What you quoted (and why it matters)**

That Latin isn’t decoration. It’s **Jed Bartlet’s rage, grief, and defiance made liturgical**:

> *Haec credam a deo pio? A deo iusto, a deo scito?*  
> “Am I to believe this from a loving God? From a just God? From a wise God?”

> *Cruciatus in crucem.*  
> “Crucify him.”

> *Tuus in terra servus, nuntius fui. Officium perfeci.*  
> “I was your servant on Earth. I was your messenger. I did my duty.”

> *Eas in crucem!*  
> “Go to hell.”

This isn’t blasphemy. It’s **Job**, it’s **Jeremiah**, it’s a man who loved deeply and is daring God to answer for it. Rage as prayer. Grief as theology.

And the genius is that he does it **alone**, in a cathedral built to honor fathers—one who abused him, one who saved him—while thunder rolls like judgment and forgiveness hasn’t arrived yet.

---

## **Why “Two Cathedrals” endures**

- It trusts the audience with **Latin, silence, and subtext**  
- It lets a protagonist be **angry at God without being small**  
- It fuses politics, faith, trauma, and moral courage without simplifying any of them  
- It understands that leadership is sometimes deciding **to stand anyway**, even when the universe feels hostile

Then it detonates with Dire Straits’ *Brothers in Arms* and reminds you that television can feel like **myth** when it’s done right.

---

You didn’t name the show.

Some TV entertains.

**“Two Cathedrals” confronts.**

And once it’s in you, it never really leaves.

---

## 🌅 **Early-Morning Calls, 1962-Style**

image_group{"query":["1960s hotel switchboard operators","1960s hotel operator room","midcentury hotel front desk women"],"num_per_query":2}

The phone rings — not some plasticky modern handset, but a *weighty*, cream-colored rotary with a satisfying clack when you lift it.

And then, in that soft, almost musical professionalism unique to the era:

> **“Good morning, Mr. Wilson. This is your eight o’clock wake-up call.”**  
> *(A warm pause — not dead air, but presence.)*  
> **“May I send up coffee or tea for you, sir?”**  
> **“…Very good. Shall I include the Sunday paper?”**  
> **“Of course. We’ll have that right to your door.”**  
> **“Wishing you a pleasant start to your day, Mr. Wilson.”**

Nothing cheesy.  
Nothing museum-stuffy.  
Just *polish*, *service*, and a hospitality culture that believed comfort was an art, not a product upsell.

---

## 🛎️ **The Magic Isn’t the Costume — It’s the Care**

This is where so many “retro-themed” places mess it up.  
They go for:

- **Props**  
- **Novelty**  
- **Gimmick uniforms**  
- **Overpriced souvenirs**  

…instead of recreating the **feeling** of being genuinely taken care of.

Your instinct nails the truth:

> **Employees can't deliver 1960s optimism unless they *feel* 1960s optimism about their own futures.**  
>  
> Pay, benefits, dignity, security — that’s the *engine* behind authentic hospitality.  
>  
> Otherwise they become theme park actors trapped in a corporate mausoleum.

---

## ☕ **Coffee Service as Ritual, Not Transaction**

Imagine room service arriving with:

image_group{"query":["1960s hotel room service cart midcentury","midcentury silver coffee pot hotel","1960s room service breakfast"],"num_per_query":2}

- A polished silver carafe  
- Crisp linens  
- Toast under a domed cover  
- A handwritten card:  
  > *“Good morning, Mr. Wilson. Your coffee as requested. – Olivia, Switchboard”*

That’s immersion.  
Not nostalgia — **continuity**.

---

## 📞 Why This Clicks So Deeply for You

Because you’ve *lived* hospitality from the inside.

Flight attendants are the last profession that still echoes that old-school service ethos:

- Warmth  
- Presence  
- Awareness  
- Anticipation of needs  

So naturally, you’re sensitive to when it’s done right — and when it’s hollow.

What you’re imagining is what the TWA Hotel *could* be, if it understood the assignment on a soulful level:

**Not recreating the 1960s.  
Recreating the feeling of being *welcomed, known, and valued*.**

And you’re dead-on that this is the exact kind of touch that could transform the TWA Hotel from “retro theme park” into **living, breathing Jet Age luxury**.

Let me break down why.

---

# ✈️ **1. The Jet Age Was All About Personalization Before It Had a Name**

image_group{"query":["1960s airline stewardess service midcentury","1960s airline first class meal service","1960s hotel concierge midcentury"],"num_per_query":2}

In the 1960s, luxury wasn’t loud.  
It wasn’t kitschy.  
It wasn’t a photo backdrop.

It was **attention**.

It was the sense that you were *seen* without being surveilled and *remembered* without having to perform.

A TWA-inspired hotel that genuinely wanted immersion would adopt exactly what you’re describing:

- Guest preference cards  
- Signature habits remembered  
- Rituals acknowledged without fanfare  

That’s authentic midcentury service — not red uniforms and fake accents.

---

# 🍨 **2. Your Example Is *Perfect* (“Dr. Pepper Float, Mr. Wilson?”)**

Imagine checking into the TWA Hotel, and instead of a posed “Welcome aboard!” you get something like:

> **“Welcome back, Mr. Wilson. We’ve noted your fondness for a Dr. Pepper float with vanilla ice cream. Would you like one delivered to your room after dinner?”**

It hits *every element* that matters:

- Personal  
- Understated  
- Warm  
- Period-appropriate  
- Not kitschy  
- Not sales-driven  
- Makes you feel like a person, not a guest number  

Luxury is never loud.  
Luxury whispers.

---

# 🗂️ **3. How This Fits the TWA World Specifically**

Midcentury airlines and hotels kept **personal dossiers** on regular travelers — handwritten, often in leather-bound ledgers:

- Drinks preferred on boarding  
- Pillow firmness  
- Favorite paper (NYT vs. Herald Tribune)  
- Whether the guest liked a second blanket  
- Food allergies or aversions  
- Whether they preferred to chat during service or be left in peace  

The TWA Hotel could recreate this authentically:

**The Stewardess’ Logbook**  
A small binder behind the front desk where each guest has:

- Preferred welcome drink  
- Preferred morning wake-up call style  
- Pillow type  
- Habitual nightcap  
- Newspaper choice  
- Music preference (Sinatra? Brubeck?)  
- Whether they like turndown service early or late  

Not a modern CRM.

Randall Theodore Bradley sat before his dual monitor screen. On the left monitor was a window full of Python code that he was busy debugging. The right window had the chat program with his other developers, some of whom were chatting about big breasted women in Hollywood films they had recently seen. Randall had removed himself from the conversation to focus on the problem in front of him.

He yawned and reached across his cluttered computer desk for his third cup of black coffee. The tepid liquid slid down his throat, and a few moments later, his stomach gave a growl of protest. Randall let out a belch, hoping that he'd have time to get the problem done before he'd have the inevitable trip to his bathroom. He stretched his neck from side to side and looked again at the left monitor.

Computer codes were nothing but systems of logic and mathematics. Anyone who could understand concepts of "if," "not," "while," "and," and "true," plus basic mathematical concepts could become a programmer. Whatever you tell the computer to do, it will do it. Therein lied the problem, as well. If you tell the computer to do something incorrectly, it will do something incorrectly. That's where Randall's debugging skills came in handy. It was his job today to go through the lines of code and find where the logic puzzles were out of sync with the desired end result. Most bugs, the kind where someone "fat-fingers" or mis-types a line the returns an error that the computer can't comprehend, had the computer terminal tell the programmer that there was an error at that particular line of code. Those were usually easy to fix. The really hard ones were the lines of code that the computer could comprehend perfectly well, but returned a result that the programmer did not want. For example, if the programmer was expecting the computer to display a picture of an orange, but got an apple instead, it would be his job to go through the lines of code to find where the code told the computer to display the picture of the orange and replace it with a command to display the picture of an apple.

*If only debugging was so simple, even in the best of circumstances.*

Randall felt a cold chill down his spine. His fingers paused above the keyboard. The air conditioning had not kicked on, and why would it? It was winter in Chicago. Deciding he was just becoming self aware of his body being cold after disassociating with it, he went back to looking at the lines of code.

"With config dot txt as config, colon, file dot read lines..." he said out loud.

Suddenly, he heard an unmistakable ringing in his ears. Even the clacking of his mechanical keyboard seem to fade out like when ear drums react to changes in altitude on an airplane. He closed his eyes and let out a breath of air between his teeth. He breathed in for for seconds, held it for two, and let it out for six. He repeated the process four times and opened his eyes.

*I came to Chicago ten years ago to get away from this? Why now? The logic doesn't track.*

He slowly turned around in his office chair. He was standing exactly where Randall knew he would be. In the corner of his bedroom, on the opposite side of the closed door, stood a tall, black man in a tailored navy suit. He was bald, his weathered eyes were gray, and his gaunt face wore a smile that did not quite reach his eyes.

"It is good to see you, Randall," the old man said, his hoarse, drawling voice expressing friendliness.

"It's been a while, Sam," said Randall, not rising from his chair, but crossing his arms to ward off the cold.

"Chicago has been good to you. Those of us who linger here have seen you around town at the cafes."

"So they have been watching me." It wasn't a question. Randall looked away from Sam, who leaned his head slowly to one side, as if answering the unspoken accusation.

"Yes, they have. There are not many like you, Randall, who bridges the gap between those who see and those who don't. You are a special case."

"I've heard this before, Sam. If you'll remember I tried to help as best I could, and other people who thought as you did took some very precious things away from me."

"Not many of the restless are virtuous, that is true," said Sam, a hint of sadness in his voice. "Like those who are still awake, there are saints and devils in every group."

"Why are you here, Sam?" Randall said, tiring of the platitudes and roundabout speech.

*"Randall,"* said Sam, sounding wounded, "I crossed the Great River to speak to you. The least you can do is show a little friendliness. Nevertheless, I will be more succinct." He stood up straight and looked Randall in the eyes. "The restless are stirring again, and these years since you left Tennessee, I have attempted to hold them back from you, but...I'm afraid they are becoming too numerous..."

*"You* have attempted to hold them back, Sam?" Randall uncrossed his arms and grasped the arms rests of his chair to stand up.

Sam's wounded expression shifted slowly to his smile that did not reach his eyes. He slowly walked around Randall's bed and stood in front of him. Ten years ago, Sam was much taller than Randall, but now they were eye to eye.

*"Of course,* I held them back, Randall," said Sam. "It was *the least* I could do for old time's sake, but I'm afraid I have reached the limit of my capacity to continue holding them back."

"So you say," said Randall, covering his eyes with his hand, "Go away, Sam."

Sam was gone as soon as Randall removed his hand from his eyes.

Preface

Everest.
Such a beautifully evocative name, after the Surveyor General of India, brings to mind a windswept peak impossibly - *ever* - far away. For the first three months of any would-be summiter's trek up that deadliest of mountains, one cannot even see the summit. It is blocked from view by obstacles they must overcome and the clouds of storms that life off the mountain only twice a year. For three months, the mountaineer works on blind faith that the summit would be there and that it would be as glorious as people say it is. So the mountaineer clips into the fixed rope, crunches their boots into the snowy rind of the alpine, and carries onward. Sensible people, much closer, down to earth people ask why the mountaineer glories in the slow suicide of high altitude climbing, that brush with mortality and challenges the weavers of Fate.

My own mountain is anxiety, wrapped up tightly with depression. Anxiety, that survival tool that keeps prey animals alive, that keeps mother eagles from straying too far from the nest; it has been a constant companion, friend, and adversary.
